lead: A learner sees a finite set of examples and must choose a rule that works on unseen cases. Usually many rules fit the training data exactly. Inductive bias is the set of assumptions that breaks the tie and picks one general rule. It is why a learner can generalize at all. Find-S, candidate elimination and decision trees each carry a different bias. In practice, bias is chosen to match the domain: spam filters, credit scoring, medical triage. The same idea appears as a prior in Bayesian learning.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for version spaces and Find-S, and Chapter 1.4 for the overfitting preview.

sections.h3: Bias chooses one rule from many

blocks.text: A hypothesis is one rule that labels examples. The hypothesis space is the set of all rules the learner is allowed to consider. With 20 emails and 10 binary features, the space can hold more than a thousand rules. Many of them fit the same 20 labels. Training data alone cannot say which one to keep.

Inductive bias is the set of assumptions a learner uses to choose one general rule among the many rules consistent with the data. Consistent means zero training error on the seen examples. The bias can be a restriction on the rule language, an order on rules, or a preference score.

Find-S has a simple bias: it keeps the most specific hypothesis. It starts from the most specific rule and generalizes only when a positive example forces it. It never generalizes beyond what the positive examples force. Candidate elimination keeps all consistent hypotheses in the version space. Its bias is the chosen hypothesis space: usually conjunctions of attribute constraints, with a most specific and a most general boundary.

A decision tree learner prefers shorter trees. A shorter tree is a simpler rule, and the preference is a bias, not a proof. This is the Occam preference. The no-free-lunch result says no learner is best on every possible task. A bias that helps on email spam may hurt on a task with reversed labels. So bias must match the domain.

sections.h3: Training error, test error and the gap

blocks.text: Generalization means performance on new examples from the same distribution. Training error measures fit on seen examples. Test error measures fit on unseen examples. A model can have low training error and high test error. That is overfitting.
training error = wrong on training ÷ n_train
blocks.where: wrong on training is the number of training examples misclassified; n_train is the number of training examples.

blocks.text: Test error uses a separate test set with n_test examples. The generalization gap is test error minus training error. Report both errors as percentages, so the gap is in percentage points.
generalization gap = test error − training error
blocks.where: the gap is in percentage points when both errors are percentages; a large positive gap signals overfitting.

blocks.text: A small gap with high training error is underfitting. A large gap with low training error is overfitting. The worked example shows two rules with the same training error but different test error.

sections.h3: Bias as a prior: the MAP view

blocks.text: Probability turns bias into a prior. A prior P(h) gives each hypothesis a starting preference before seeing data. The likelihood P(D | h) says how well h explains data D. The posterior P(h | D) combines both.

blocks.where: P(h | D) is the posterior probability of hypothesis h after data D; P(D | h) is the likelihood of the data under h; P(h) is the prior probability of h; ∝ means proportional to.

blocks.text: MAP learning picks the single hypothesis with the largest posterior. The prior is the inductive bias. A prior that prefers short decision trees makes MAP prefer shorter trees. Full Bayes averages over many hypotheses instead of picking one; see Unit 3, Classification: Trees, Bayes, kNN, SVM.
h_MAP = argmax_h [log P(D | h) + log P(h)]
blocks.where: h_MAP is the chosen hypothesis; argmax_h picks the h with the largest value; log turns products into sums.

examples.question: Two hypotheses h1 and h2 both fit 20 training emails with 18 correct. h1 is a complex rule with 30 conditions; h2 has 3 conditions. On 100 test emails, h1 is correct on 65 and h2 on 80. Compute training error, test error and the generalization gap for each.
steps: Training errors: h1 is wrong on 20 − 18 = 2 emails, so 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = 10%. h2 is also wrong on 2 emails, so 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = 10%.
Test errors: h1 is wrong on 100 − 65 = 35 emails, so 35 ÷ 100 × 100 = 35%. h2 is wrong on 100 − 80 = 20 emails, so 20 ÷ 100 × 100 = 20%.
Generalization gaps: h1 gap = 35% − 10% = 25 percentage points. h2 gap = 20% − 10% = 10 percentage points.
The simpler h2 has the smaller gap, so the complexity preference is a useful inductive bias here.
examples.answer: h1: training error 10%, test error 35%, gap 25 percentage points. h2: training error 10%, test error 20%, gap 10 percentage points. h2 generalizes better.

traps: Saying a learner has no bias. Every learner that generalizes beyond seen data has some inductive bias.
Confusing inductive bias with statistical bias or the bias term in the bias-variance trade-off. They are different ideas.
Reporting training error as if it were generalization. Always state test error and the gap.
Writing a gap of 25% when the errors are percentages. The gap is 25 percentage points, not 25 percent.
Assuming the shorter tree is always better. Occam preference is a bias, not a guarantee; test data decides.

quiz.q: Define inductive bias in one sentence.
quiz.a: Inductive bias is the set of assumptions a learner uses to choose one general rule among many rules consistent with the training data.

quiz.q: Why is it wrong to say a learning algorithm has no inductive bias?
quiz.a: Any algorithm that chooses a rule for unseen examples must prefer some rules over others. Without a preference, all consistent rules remain equally valid and no single general rule can be chosen.

quiz.q: A model is correct on 45 of 50 training examples and on 150 of 200 test examples. Compute training error, test error and the generalization gap.
quiz.a: Training error = (50 − 45) ÷ 50 × 100 = 10%. Test error = (200 − 150) ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%. Gap = 25% − 10% = 15 percentage points.

quiz.q: Find-S keeps the most specific hypothesis; candidate elimination keeps the version space. Which part of each method is its inductive bias?
quiz.a: Find-S bias is the preference for the most specific consistent hypothesis. Candidate elimination's bias is the chosen hypothesis space — conjunctions of attribute constraints — and the assumption that the target concept lies in that space. The general-to-specific ordering is only a representation tool for tracking the version space; it is not the bias itself.

quiz.q: In the MAP formula, what role does the prior P(h) play?
quiz.a: The prior gives each hypothesis a starting preference before data. It acts as the inductive bias, so MAP prefers hypotheses with higher prior even when likelihoods are close.

quiz.q: Two decision trees have the same training error. Tree A is much larger and has much higher test error than tree B. What does this show about bias and generalization?
quiz.a: Tree A has the larger generalization gap. Whether that counts as overfitting depends on the training-error level: if both trees have low training error, tree A is overfitting, and if training error is high, both are underfitting and the gap is not the whole story. Here the preference for shorter trees is supported, because tree B performs better on test data.

quiz.q: A decision tree learner prefers shorter trees. Is that a restriction on the hypothesis space or a preference over hypotheses?
quiz.a: It is a preference over hypotheses. Longer trees are still allowed, but shorter trees are chosen first when both fit the data.

beyond: Not for the exam. Formal learning theory uses VC dimension and PAC bounds to quantify how much data a hypothesis space needs. Bayesian model averaging replaces MAP's single choice with a weighted vote over hypotheses. Modern deep networks show implicit bias from architecture and gradient descent, even without an explicit simplicity penalty. Search for VC dimension, PAC learning, Bayesian model averaging and implicit regularization to go deeper.
